title: The $300 You'd Save on Insurance Could Cost You $1,500 -- Here's the Math
hook: A cheaper insurance plan with a bigger deductible isn't automatically the better deal -- here's the exact claim frequency where it stops paying off.
description:
Plan A: $1,100/year premium, $500 deductible. Plan B: $800/year premium, $2,000 deductible. Plan B looks like the obvious pick until you do the expected-value math on how often you'd actually file a claim. We run the numbers on exactly where the break-even point sits.

This video uses AI-generated narration and visuals.

#Shorts #insurance #personalfinance #expectedvalue

segments.text: Two insurance plans. Plan A: eleven hundred dollars a year, five hundred dollar deductible. Plan B: eight hundred dollars a year, two thousand dollar deductible.
Plan B saves you three hundred dollars a year you don't file a claim. But file one, and you're on the hook for fifteen hundred dollars more than Plan A.
So which is actually cheaper? It depends how often you expect to file a claim -- and there's an exact break-even point.
The savings equal the extra risk at exactly a twenty percent chance of a claim each year -- about once every five years.
Expect claims less often than that -- say a fifteen percent chance a year -- and Plan B wins: eleven hundred dollars versus eleven hundred seventy five.

slide.headline: Expected annual cost at a 15% claim chance

segments.text: Expect claims more often -- a forty percent chance a year -- and Plan A wins instead: thirteen hundred dollars versus sixteen hundred.

slide.headline: Expected annual cost at a 40% claim chance

segments.text: The cheaper premium isn't always cheaper. Do the expected-value math first.

lines: The cheaper premium isn't always cheaper.
